query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a small amount of carbon (0.1 at.%) to refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) can improve their high-temperature oxygen resistance by forming stable carbides, such as Ta3C and Nb3C, which can act as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) in its as-cast or homogenized condition
generation.intervention: Addition of 0.1 at.% carbon to the RHEA
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of stable carbides, such as Ta3C and Nb3C
generation.mechanism: The formation of carbides can act as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, reducing the oxidation rate of the RHEA
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature oxygen resistance, with a reduction in oxidation rate and an increase in the alloy's lifespan
generation.baseline: The oxidation rate of the RHEA without the addition of carbon
generation.boundary: The temperature and pressure conditions under which the carbides are stable and can act as an effective barrier to oxygen diffusion
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism by which the carbides form and interact with the RHEA, as well as the optimal amount of carbon to add

falsification_experiment.design: Expose the carbon-doped RHEA to high-temperature (above 800°C) and high-pressure (above 6 GPa) conditions and measure the oxidation rate
measurements: Microstructural analysis to confirm the formation of carbides
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidation rate of the carbon-doped RHEA is not significantly reduced compared to the undoped RHEA, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: In this work, the formation of carbide with the concertation of carbon at 0.1 at.% in refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20 was studied under both ambient and high-pressure high-temperature conditions. The x-ray diffraction of dilute carbon (C)-doped RHEA under ambient pressure showed that the phases and lattice constant of RHEA were not influenced by the addition of 0.1 at.% C. In contrast, C-doped RHEA showed unexpected phase formation and transformation under combined high-pressure and high-temperature conditions by resistively employing the heated diamond anvil cell (DAC) technique. The new FCC_L12 phase appeared at 6 GPa and 809 °C and preserved the ambient temperature and pressure. High-pressure and high-temperature promoted the formation of carbides Ta3C and Nb3C, which are stable and may further improve the mechanical performance of the dilute C-doped alloy Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20.
